question: Which is better: renunciation of actions (karma-saṃnyāsa) or the yoga of action (karma-yoga)?

sides.label: renunciation of actions (saṃnyāsa; the 'Sāṃkhyas' of 5.4–5)
sides.position: Renunciation of actions, which Arjuna hears praised alongside yoga (5.1), brings the highest good (5.2); the place reached by the Sāṃkhyas is reached by the Yogins too (5.5); renouncing all actions by the mind the embodied one dwells at ease (5.13).
arguments: Kṛṣṇa himself praises renunciation of actions (5.1)
the Sāṃkhyas reach the same place as the Yogins (5.5)

sides.label: the yoga of action (karma-yoga)
sides.position: The yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action (5.2); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, while the sage yoked in yoga soon reaches Brahman (5.6); the true renouncer is the one who does required action without depending on its fruit, not the one without fires and rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga (6.2).
arguments: renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6)
true renunciation is inner — of fruit and intention — not outward abandonment of rites (6.1–2)
the constant renouncer is simply one who neither hates nor craves (5.3)

text_answer: The Gītā answers within the text: both lead to the highest good, but karma-yoga is superior (5.2); only children call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate, since established in either one gains the fruit of both (5.4–5); action is the means for one wishing to ascend to yoga and calm for one who has ascended (6.3).

reconciliation.explanation: The text itself says both reach the same goal (5.2, 5.4–5) and ties the means to the student's stage — action for one ascending, calm for one ascended (6.3); commentators still divide on whether the superiority of karma-yoga in 5.2 is relative to stage or absolute.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The commentarial traditions do not accept a simple equivalence: e.g. Śaṅkara takes renunciation grounded in knowledge as final and karma-yoga as preparatory for one who lacks knowledge, while Rāmānuja takes karma-yoga as superior because easier and inclusive of knowledge of the self.

notes: A question posed within the text (Arjuna, 5.1; cf. 3.1–2) and answered by Kṛṣṇa; both sides are stated as the text presents them. Related to the wider debate dsp:works-knowledge-grace.
